title: Exodus 20
literarySetting: Israel stands at Sinai after the exodus from Egypt. The chapter follows the preparation described in Exodus 19.
speakerOrNarrator: Exodus 20:1 introduces God as speaking the words; narrative description resumes in Exodus 20:18.
tabletContext: The chapter presents the spoken formulations. Exodus 24:12 and 31:18 later connect divine instruction with stone tablets.

structuralSections.label: Commands commonly identified as the Decalogue

distinctiveThemes: The exodus is stated in the opening identification
The Sabbath rationale points to creation

observations.summary: God speaks the words introduced in Exodus 20:1.
Jewish and Christian traditions commonly identify Exodus 20:2–17 as a Decalogue formulation, while differing in enumeration.

notes: Reference and structural metadata only; biblical text is not duplicated.

title: Exodus 34
literarySetting: The chapter follows the golden calf incident, Moses’ breaking of the first tablets, and his intercession.
speakerOrNarrator: The chapter alternates narrative and divine speech; Moses writes covenant words according to Exodus 34:27.
tabletContext: Moses cuts replacement tablets. Exodus 34:1 says words from the first tablets will be written on them; Exodus 34:28 associates the tablets with the words of the covenant and the Ten Words.

structuralSections.label: Writing, forty days, and the Ten Words

distinctiveThemes: Replacement tablets after the golden calf breach
Commands concerning covenant relations with inhabitants of the land

observations.summary: Moses broke the first tablets after seeing the calf and dancing.
The replacement tablets are to receive the words that were on the first tablets.
Exodus 34:10–26 contains a sequence of covenant commands.
Exodus 34:27 refers to “these words,” and verse 28 refers to “the words of the covenant, the Ten Words.”
The precise referent of the phrases in Exodus 34:27–28 and their relationship to the preceding commands are interpreted differently.

notes: The comparison does not claim that Exodus 34 replaces Exodus 20 or that the passages are identical.

title: Deuteronomy 5
literarySetting: In Moab, Moses addresses Israel’s next generation and recalls the covenant made at Horeb.
speakerOrNarrator: Moses narrates the Horeb setting and recites the covenant words to Israel.
tabletContext: Moses says the words were written on two stone tablets and given to him.

structuralSections.label: Call to hear and covenant setting
God’s response and call to obedience

distinctiveThemes: The Sabbath rationale points to Israel’s deliverance from slavery
Wife and house are expressed separately in the coveting command

observations.summary: Moses recalls the covenant made at Horeb and addresses Israel.
The words are said to have been written on two stone tablets.
Jewish and Christian traditions commonly identify Deuteronomy 5:6–21 as a Decalogue formulation, while differing in enumeration.

notes: Reference and structural metadata only; biblical text is not duplicated.

title: Genesis 12
literarySetting: Abram is called to leave land, kindred, and father’s house for a land God will show him.

comparisonFacts.label: Promise elements
comparisonFacts.value: Great nation, blessing, great name, becoming a blessing

comparisonFacts.label: Covenant terminology
comparisonFacts.value: The word covenant is not used in this passage

comparisonFacts.label: Ritual or sign
comparisonFacts.value: None stated

comparisonFacts.label: Named descendants
comparisonFacts.value: None named

comparisonFacts.label: Land language
comparisonFacts.value: A land God will show Abram

comparisonFacts.label: Nations language
comparisonFacts.value: All families of the earth are included in the blessing statement

comparisonFacts.label: Human response or obligation
comparisonFacts.value: Abram is commanded to go

comparisonFacts.label: Later biblical reuse
comparisonFacts.value: Acts 3:25–26; Galatians 3:8

distinctiveThemes: The sequence begins with a call to leave
The destination is not yet geographically defined

observations.summary: Nation, blessing, name, and families-of-the-earth language appear before Genesis explicitly calls the arrangement a covenant.

notes: Developmental metadata only; this entry does not claim that later passages replace this promise.

title: Genesis 15
literarySetting: Abram remains childless after the events of Genesis 14 and asks about an heir.

comparisonFacts.label: Promise elements
comparisonFacts.value: A biological heir, innumerable offspring, future deliverance, land

comparisonFacts.label: Covenant terminology
comparisonFacts.value: Genesis 15:18 explicitly says God made a covenant with Abram

comparisonFacts.label: Ritual or sign
comparisonFacts.value: Divided animals; smoking fire pot and flaming torch pass between the pieces

comparisonFacts.label: Named descendants
comparisonFacts.value: No son is named; the heir is said to come from Abram

comparisonFacts.label: Land language
comparisonFacts.value: Boundaries from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates are specified

comparisonFacts.label: Nations language
comparisonFacts.value: No families-of-the-earth formula in this chapter

comparisonFacts.label: Human response or obligation
comparisonFacts.value: Abram believes; the chapter records his preparation of the animals

comparisonFacts.label: Later biblical reuse
comparisonFacts.value: Romans 4; Galatians 3; James 2:23

distinctiveThemes: A formal ceremony with divided animals

observations.summary: Genesis 15:6 reports Abram’s belief, and Genesis 15:18 explicitly identifies covenant-making.

notes: Developmental metadata only; this entry does not claim that later passages replace this covenant ceremony.

title: Genesis 17
literarySetting: Abram is ninety-nine, and the chapter precedes Isaac’s conception and birth.

comparisonFacts.label: Promise elements
comparisonFacts.value: Numerous nations, kings, land, divine relationship, Isaac

comparisonFacts.label: Covenant terminology
comparisonFacts.value: Covenant language is repeated throughout; everlasting language is used

comparisonFacts.label: Ritual or sign
comparisonFacts.value: Circumcision is commanded as the covenant sign

comparisonFacts.label: Named descendants
comparisonFacts.value: Isaac and Ishmael are both named; the covenant is specified with Isaac

comparisonFacts.label: Land language
comparisonFacts.value: Canaan is described as an everlasting possession

comparisonFacts.label: Nations language
comparisonFacts.value: Abraham is called father of a multitude of nations; Sarah is connected with nations and kings

comparisonFacts.label: Human response or obligation
comparisonFacts.value: Walk before God, be blameless, keep the covenant, circumcise the household

comparisonFacts.label: Later biblical reuse
comparisonFacts.value: Acts 7:8; Romans 4:9–12

observations.summary: Genesis 17 contains both divine promises and commands addressed to Abraham and his household.

notes: The record identifies textual elements without resolving later disputes concerning descendants, land, or duration.

title: Genesis 22
literarySetting: Abraham is tested concerning Isaac after Isaac’s birth and after the separation of Hagar and Ishmael.

comparisonFacts.label: Promise elements
comparisonFacts.value: Blessing, multiplied offspring, possession of enemy gates, blessing among nations

comparisonFacts.label: Covenant terminology
comparisonFacts.value: The word covenant is not used; the divine speech includes an oath

comparisonFacts.label: Ritual or sign
comparisonFacts.value: Isaac is bound; a ram is offered in his place

comparisonFacts.label: Named descendants
comparisonFacts.value: Isaac is the named son involved in the test

comparisonFacts.label: Land language
comparisonFacts.value: No territorial boundaries are stated here

comparisonFacts.label: Nations language
comparisonFacts.value: All nations of the earth are included in the blessing statement

comparisonFacts.label: Human response or obligation
comparisonFacts.value: The oath speech states that Abraham obeyed God’s voice

comparisonFacts.label: Later biblical reuse
comparisonFacts.value: Hebrews 6:13–20; Hebrews 11:17–19; James 2:21–23

observations.summary: The oath follows Abraham’s action and repeats earlier offspring and nations themes with explicit obedience language.

notes: This entry presents the oath as a later stage in Genesis and does not claim that it replaces earlier promises or the Genesis 15 covenant ceremony.
